messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That might refer to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis. Usually we compute the standard error as sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That would be sigma/sqrt(n) where sigma is the population standard deviation. But we don't have population standard deviation; we have sample standard deviation. So we approximate using sample standard deviation.

Thus standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. So about 0.22.

But the user might want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? They might want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic is sqrt((n-1)/(n-3))? Actually the t distribution has variance n/(n-2) for df=n-1. But that's not typical. They might just want the standard error.

Thus answer: approximately 0.2215.

We can also compute the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test statistic: t = (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is the standard error. So the standard deviation of the t-statistic is sqrt(df/(df-2))? But we don't need that.

Thus answer: ~0.22.

We can provide explanation.
